blocks.text: .2 Budget as a Policy Tool and as a Managerial Tool

segments.text: , the budget reveals which sectors and programs actually receive resources, and revenue decisions (who is taxed, and how much) are themselves a form of policy, affecting the distribution of the tax burden across society. As a

, budgets let managers plan activities, allocate resources deliberately, control spending against authorized limits, and compare actual performance against planned targets — the same planning-and-control logic introduced in the Management unit of the Business Administration chapter, now applied within the specific legal constraints of public budget law.

blocks.text: .3 Principles of Budgeting, Audit, and Accounting

segments.text: Sound budgeting should be lawful (within statutory authority), transparent (open to legislative and public scrutiny), realistic (grounded in credible revenue and cost estimates), and accountable (traceable to responsible officials).

(examines adherence to applicable rules and regulations), and

Each budgeting system below answers a different underlying question, and remembering that governing question is the fastest way to keep all five distinct:

items.text: asks “how much will be spent on each input?” — organizing spending by input categories (salaries, supplies, equipment). It provides strong, easily auditable input control but says relatively little directly about what results that spending actually buys.

asks “what performance will this spending produce?” — linking resources to activities, outputs, or performance indicators (a road-maintenance unit’s budget connected to kilometres maintained and response times, rather than only to labour and materials cost). Its central challenge is selecting genuinely valid measures and avoiding incentives that reward “chasing easy numbers” rather than real performance improvement.

asks “which program or policy objective is this spending funding?” — grouping resources around programs or purposes rather than administrative input categories, making it easier to ask how various activities jointly contribute to one policy objective.

asks “why should this activity exist at all, starting from zero?” — requiring every activity to be freshly justified each budget cycle, rather than assuming the previous year’s spending base automatically continues forward. Its acknowledged practical limitation is the heavy analytical burden of comprehensively re-justifying every activity in a large government, which is why fully zero-based budgeting is rarely sustained in its pure form for long.

asks “what change in society do we actually want, beyond outputs delivered?” — connecting spending to broader societal outcomes rather than only to immediate activities or deliverables. Its central difficulty, echoing the attribution problem already raised in program evaluation above, is that outcomes are typically shaped by many actors and external conditions beyond the specific program’s control, making it genuinely hard to isolate how much of an observed societal change is actually attributable to this specific budget line.

The practical coordination challenge, worth naming explicitly, is ensuring that development spending (new schools, new clinics) is properly matched with the recurrent budget needed to actually staff and operate those new facilities once built — a frequent real-world failure mode where new infrastructure is built without adequately budgeting for its ongoing operational costs.

items.text: Each of the five budgeting systems answers a different governing question — memorize the question, not just the label, since exam scenarios often describe a budgeting approach without naming it and expect the correct label to be identified.

Financial, compliance, and performance/value-for-money audit are three distinct examinations of the same spending, asking different questions (accuracy, rule-adherence, and economy/efficiency/effectiveness respectively).

Development spending (new capital projects) and recurrent spending (ongoing operating costs) must be planned together — new infrastructure without matching recurrent budget for its operation is a recurring real-world budgeting failure.
